name: IAB TCF consent string
plain: A coded record of which ad vendors and purposes the person agreed to in the EU consent banner.
meaning: Stored in the euconsent-v2 cookie and read through __tcfapi. TCF v2.3 requires the disclosedVendors segment, and strings without it were invalid from Feb 28 2026. Consent is valid for up to 13 months.

access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can see which ad vendors you agreed to in the EU cookie banner
limits.user_action: You tap Accept, Reject, or Manage choices on a cookie banner
can: Check which ad vendors and purposes you said yes to
Pass your choices along to the ad partners it works with
Remember your answer for up to 13 months
Show the banner again if the record is missing or out of date
cannot: Count a choice you never made as your consent
Use a record that lacks the vendor list; since Feb 28 2026 those strings are invalid
Keep your choices past 13 months without asking again
Tell vendors you agreed when you picked Reject all
limits.reach_label: Only choices you made in the banner

story.what_it_is: A saved note of which ad companies and purposes you said yes or no to on a cookie banner.

marketing.name: Transparency and Consent Framework
marketing.pitch: The industry standard that lets sites, ad vendors and consent banners share one record of what a person agreed to.

story.for_you: You see it as the cookie banner in Europe, with a button to accept, reject or manage choices. After you tap, the site stores a coded note of your answers. Ad companies on the page read that note instead of asking you again.
story.for_makers: Publishers and ad vendors need proof that a person agreed before personal data is used for ads. The string travels with every ad request, so each buyer knows what it may do. It also keeps a paper trail for regulators.

use_cases.example: A European newspaper shows a banner, then passes your choices to every ad vendor on the page so only allowed ones load.
In a real-time ad auction, the exchange reads the string first and drops bidders that were not approved.
A free browser games portal shows a consent banner on first visit and only runs personalised ads between rounds if you agreed.
A streaming site plays a generic pre-roll ad instead of a targeted one when you reject the banner.
A measurement tag waits for the consent note before it fires, so rejected visitors are not counted individually.
A web shop only loads retargeting pixels from vendors you ticked, so you do not see its ads follow you around.
A compliance team keeps logs of consent strings to show a regulator that a visitor really said yes.

risks: Consent claims that regulators have challenged

technical_bounds: Covers 11 purposes and 3 special purposes plus vendor IDs
Not a legal proof by itself

abuse: Weak consent flows (CNIL and Belgian DPA rulings on TCF)

history.change: TCF v2.2 removed legitimate interest for some purposes
TCF v2.3 with disclosedVendors mandatory from Feb 28 2026
